I coordinate open calls for a residency program, and every year I read around four hundred applications. The first thing I want to say is simple: read the eligibility section twice. About one in ten applications is disqualified before anybody looks at the art, because the applicant is not eligible or a mandatory document is missing. The second thing is the difference between must and should. When a call says you must include a budget, it is not a suggestion. When it says you should include a letter of support, nobody will reject you without one, but the strongest applications usually have it. And when it says you do not have to have a degree, please believe it. Some of our best residents never went to art school. What we look for is a track record, a clear proposal, and evidence that you have thought about the people you will work with.

I sit on the panel for a hospital that hosts one artist every year, and I am the clinician in the room. I want to explain why our open call has so many rules about consent. When an artist records a patient, the patient is required to sign a form, and the artist is expected to explain, in plain language, what will happen to the recording. That is not bureaucracy. A patient on a ward is not in the same position as a visitor in a gallery. They cannot always leave, and they may feel they have to say yes. So when we shortlist applicants, one of our three criteria is care. We do not need a perfect ethics plan at that stage. We need to see that the artist has asked the right questions. An application that does not mention consent at all tells me the artist has not imagined the ward yet.
